strengths: CASA addresses an important vision-language modeling problem with a simple, implementable architectural change: text queries attend jointly to visual tokens and local text tokens, while visual tokens bypass the language model’s FFNs. Assessed as Algorithms/General, this offers a useful accuracy–efficiency tradeoff without requiring state-of-the-art benchmark performance.

The strongest evidence is the controlled comparison in Table 6. CASA⊕ improves the aggregate score from 40.3 for cross-attention and 41.5 for gated cross-attention to 65.4, with particularly large gains on document/chart understanding and OCR. These experiments support the architectural contribution more convincingly than comparisons against separately trained published models.

Evaluation covers two relevant settings—building a VLM from Helium1 and adapting Qwen2.5-VL—and a broad range of image and video benchmarks. Ablations examine layer placement, visual FFN updates, token compression, and attention masking, providing useful practical guidance.

The streaming application demonstrates a plausible practical benefit: replacing visual context avoids accumulating historical image tokens in the language-model cache. The measured memory and latency trends, public training-data descriptions, and implementation details strengthen the contribution. Overall, the demonstrated improvement over cross-attention supports a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The claim of largely closing the gap to token insertion needs qualification, particularly for the fine-detail tasks motivating the paper. In Table 2, CASA→ scores 48.6 versus 61.8 on InfoVQA and 73.4 versus 81.6 on ChartQA. Adapting Qwen2.5-VL reduces InfoVQA from 71.6 to 59.6 and MME from 2249 to 1918 (Table 3). These are meaningful losses, and the reported average percentage drops obscure their magnitude.

The overall accuracy–efficiency comparison is not fully controlled. CASA receives approximately 0.3T training tokens versus 0.1T for the insertion baseline, with higher training resolution and larger sequence budgets. These are understandable consequences of memory constraints, but they do not isolate architectural effects or establish a matched-compute tradeoff. Table 1 also compares training times under different workloads. The controlled CASA-versus-cross-attention result remains valuable, but stronger conclusions about insertion require matched-budget comparisons.

The efficiency analysis contains substantive ambiguities. Table 1 gives CASA⊕ a T² + N(N + T_W) attention-memory expression, despite the stated linear dependence on image-token count and the absence of image queries; W in the CASA∨ expression is not clearly defined. Attention-score complexity also needs separation from actual FlashAttention memory. Table 11 reports slightly slower inference for CASA⊕ in its tested setting, so speed advantages should be stated conditionally. The formulas and measurements need a consistent account of prefill, decoding, visual-cache storage, and text-cache growth.

The implicit-gating explanation is plausible but not established as the cause of improvement. Masking self-attention only at inference introduces a distribution shift and shows reliance on that pathway, rather than proving why it helped during training. A trained variant attending to images plus only the current text token would help distinguish self-preservation from interactions among different text tokens. Figure 7 compares per-token attention averages rather than total attention mass by modality, further limiting the mechanistic interpretation.

The streaming evaluation does not fully test the information-retention tradeoff. CASA discards direct access to earlier visual windows, yet there is no targeted evaluation of revisiting earlier images or recovering previously unmentioned details. Offline video QA places the entire video in one window, whereas LiveSports3K evaluates roughly 20-second clips; neither establishes long-horizon streaming quality. Efficiency comparisons also omit the cited cache-pruning or memory-based streaming approaches. This limits claims that insertion-based streaming is prohibitively costly and that CASA preserves long-context capabilities.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, CASA offers a simple, useful modification to vision-language fusion: text queries attend jointly to image tokens and local text tokens without forwarding images through the language model’s FFNs. The practical contribution does not depend on achieving the highest benchmark accuracy.

The controlled comparison in Table 6 provides strong evidence of improvement over conventional cross-attention. CASA achieves 65.4 average versus 40.3 for ordinary cross-attention and 41.5 for gated cross-attention, with particularly large gains on document/chart understanding and OCR.

Experiments cover training from a text-only backbone, adapting an existing VLM, image and video benchmarks, and streaming captioning. Ablations examine layer placement, image-feature updates, token compression, and attention masking, giving the central architectural proposal substantial empirical support.

The efficiency motivation is credible: excluding visual tokens from language-model FFNs and retaining only the current visual window reduces important costs. Table 11 and Figures 5–6 demonstrate practical benefits, especially as streaming sequences grow. The appendix also provides useful dataset, preprocessing, and training details.
weaknesses: The remaining accuracy gap is substantial on some of the very tasks motivating the paper. In Table 2, CASA→ scores 48.6 versus 61.8 on InfoVQA and 73.4 versus 81.6 on ChartQA. Adapting Qwen2.5-VL reduces InfoVQA from 71.6 to 59.6 and MME from 2249 to 1918 (Table 3). These results support a useful efficiency–accuracy tradeoff, but the broad language about closing the gap and small performance drops understates important regressions.

The mechanistic explanation is not fully isolated. Removing self-attention at inference establishes that a trained model relies on that connection, but does not establish that implicit gating, rather than additional text processing or initialization effects, causes the improvement. Training comparisons against current-token-only attention and separately normalized text/visual attention would be informative. Figure 7 compares per-token attention averages rather than total modality mass, limiting its support for the gating interpretation.

The efficiency analysis contains a material inconsistency: Table 1 gives CASA⊕ a term N(N + T_W), despite defining N as image-token count and claiming linear scaling because images are never queries. The CASA∨ expression also uses an insufficiently defined W. These formulas need correction and a clear distinction between attention computation, activation memory with FlashAttention, and KV-cache storage. Table 11 additionally shows CASA⊕ slightly slower than insertion in its inference setting, so speed advantages should be qualified by workload.

Several comparisons do not isolate architecture under matched budgets. Table 2 reports approximately 0.3T training tokens for CASA versus 0.1T for the insertion baseline, alongside different training resolutions and sequence caps. The controlled cross-attention ablation remains valuable, but its shortened schedule and baseline configuration are insufficiently specified to assess convergence. A matched-budget accuracy–efficiency comparison would strengthen the broader conclusions.

Streaming evaluation establishes resource scaling more convincingly than long-horizon visual understanding. Caption quality is evaluated on approximately 20-second clips, while efficiency is measured over much longer streams. Replacing earlier visual windows also removes direct access to prior images, but no targeted evaluation measures the resulting historical-information loss. Comparisons with cache-pruned or memory-based streaming methods are missing, and the qualitative comparison in Appendix D uses different backbones. These gaps limit the streaming claims, although they do not negate the strong controlled evidence for improved fusion.

strengths: CASA offers a simple, useful architectural contribution: adding local causal text-to-text attention to visual cross-attention while keeping image tokens out of the language model’s main processing stream. Evaluated as an Algorithms/General paper, its contribution is a practical accuracy–efficiency trade-off rather than a new benchmark record.

The strongest evidence is the controlled comparison in Table 6. CASA achieves 66.4 HRES and 72.3 OCR, versus 32.0 and 32.2 for gated cross-attention under the stated identical training settings. These substantial improvements support the central claim that the proposed fusion mechanism addresses weaknesses of conventional cross-attention.

The evaluation covers training from a text-only backbone, adapting a pretrained VLM, nine image benchmarks, video understanding, and streaming captioning. Ablations examine fusion placement, image-feature updates, token compression, and attention masking, providing useful architectural guidance.

The efficiency benefits have a credible structural basis and practical support: image tokens bypass language-model FFNs, and past visual windows can be discarded. The streaming measurements and supplementary profiling demonstrate meaningful memory savings. Public training datasets, named evaluation tools, and detailed supplementary configurations also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The remaining accuracy gap is substantial on precisely the fine-detail tasks motivating the work. In Table 2, CASA→ scores 48.6 versus 61.8 on InfoVQA and 73.4 versus 81.6 on ChartQA for the insertion baseline. In Table 3, adapting Qwen2.5-VL reduces InfoVQA from 71.6 to 59.6 and MME from 2249 to 1918. Descriptions such as closing the gap or retaining nearly all performance should be qualified by task; aggregate percentage drops obscure important losses.

Comparisons with insertion do not cleanly isolate the architectural trade-off. CASA and insertion use different training resolutions and sequence budgets, and Table 2 reports approximately 0.3T versus 0.1T training tokens. These are understandable hardware-driven choices, but matched-data and matched-compute comparisons are needed to characterize the accuracy–efficiency frontier. Comparisons with external models additionally involve different backbones and training recipes.

The implicit-gating explanation is plausible but not conclusively established. Masking self-attention only at inference demonstrates reliance on a learned pathway, while also introducing distribution shift. It does not establish whether the gain requires interaction with other text tokens, attending only to the current token, or additional textual transformations. Training a self-token-only variant and a comparably expressive gating baseline would substantially strengthen the mechanistic claim.

The strongest long-stream claims exceed the quality evaluation. LiveSports3K contains approximately 20-second clips, whereas efficiency is measured over much longer streams. Discarding previous visual windows can sacrifice information needed for later questions, and no targeted evaluation measures that loss. Textual cache growth also remains. Comparisons against streaming systems with cache eviction or visual memory, alongside long-duration grounding and temporal-recall tests, would make the practical case more convincing.

The efficiency analysis needs clarification. Table 1 gives CASA⊕ a term N(N + T_W), despite defining N as image-token count and claiming linear scaling in image tokens; W in the CASA∨ expression is not clearly defined. Attention-score complexity should also be distinguished from actual FlashAttention memory usage. Table 11 reports slightly slower inference for CASA⊕ in its tested setting, so speed claims should explicitly identify the workloads where gains occur. These issues weaken the precision of the analysis, although they do not negate the measured memory benefits.

strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical reassessment of cross-attention for vision-language fusion. Under Algorithms/General, its main contribution is the controlled architectural study rather than a fundamentally new attention mechanism; this is a worthwhile contribution to efficient visual understanding.

The Helium experiments provide the strongest evidence: token insertion and cross-attention use the same backbone, vision encoder, data pipeline, and approximately matched training-token budgets. Table 2 shows competitive performance across nine benchmarks, including DocVQA scores of 85.8 versus 87.2 and TextVQA scores of 73.8 versus 74.4.

The study covers complementary settings: training from a text-only backbone, adapting a pretrained VLM, video QA, and streaming captioning. The parameter-sharing, layer-replacement, image-update, and Q-Former ablations provide useful practical guidance beyond a single model comparison.

The efficiency benefits are substantial in the measured setting: Table 1 reports 6.8 versus 1.2 FPS and 6.1 versus 29.5 memory units for vanilla cross-attention versus insertion. The manuscript also acknowledges task-dependent accuracy losses and provides substantial training and dataset details.
weaknesses: The streaming comparisons conflate fusion architecture with visual-history retention. Windowed cross-attention discards previous frame features, while the insertion and Q-Former baselines accumulate them. Comparisons against insertion with cache eviction or bounded visual memory are needed to establish the advantage over practical streaming alternatives. Moreover, text and gist tokens still accumulate, so near-constant memory and latency describe the measured horizon rather than an asymptotic property; Figure 4(b) plots cumulative walltime, not memory or per-frame latency.

The accuracy cost of converting a pretrained VLM is sometimes understated. Against the reproduced Qwen2.5-VL baseline, vanilla CA drops from 75.1 to 57.4 on InfoVQA, 79.6 to 74.0 on AI2D, and 2224 to 1910 on MME. These are meaningful losses despite stronger retention on other tasks. Comparisons to prior CA models also differ in pretraining, data, and resolution, so they do not isolate the architectural source of improvement.

Long-duration captioning quality is not established. Quantitative evaluation uses approximately 20-second sports clips, whereas the efficiency argument concerns much longer streams. The qualitative examples contain factual errors, including calling a pangolin a reptile, and unsupported specifics. Longer evaluations of grounding, temporal recall, and hallucination would strengthen the practical claim.

Several efficiency and causal-analysis details remain incomplete. Table 1 does not clearly specify the history length underlying its inference measurements, memory units, or full timing configuration, and total parameter counts after adding CA are not reported. The five-factor decomposition is informative but is not validated through a complete progressive reconstruction of insertion; notably, visual self-attention updates are not isolated experimentally.

Reproducibility and presentation need corrections: the supplied manuscript has no usable project-page link despite release claims, small performance differences lack uncertainty estimates, and some references and labels are inconsistent. For example, reference [44], cited for visual context compression, concerns 3D medical volume contrastive learning, and Appendix B.2 lists resolutions inconsistent with Table 8. These are secondary concerns rather than the main reason for the borderline recommendation.

strengths: The paper provides a useful empirical reassessment of cross-attention for vision-language fusion. Under Algorithms/General, its main contribution is the controlled comparison and practical adaptation strategy; the absence of a fundamentally new attention mechanism does not negate this value.

The Helium experiments provide the strongest evidence: cross-attention and token insertion share the backbone, visual encoder, training data, and approximately matched token budgets. Table 2 demonstrates competitive performance across nine benchmarks while exposing remaining weaknesses on chart and infographic understanding.

The efficiency improvements are substantial in the reported configuration. Table 1 shows vanilla cross-attention reducing training memory from 62.8 to 32.9 and increasing streaming throughput from 1.2 to 6.8 FPS. Parameter sharing and alternating attention layers offer additional useful trade-offs.

The study covers both training from a text-only backbone and adapting a pretrained VLM, with image, video, and streaming evaluations. The architectural decomposition, attention diagrams, and appendix provide useful implementation guidance, and the paper explicitly acknowledges the trade-off from discarding direct access to past images.
weaknesses: The streaming comparison conflates fusion architecture with visual-history retention. The proposed model retains only the latest frame directly, whereas insertion baselines accumulate visual tokens. Although this is a legitimate design choice, comparisons against insertion models with cache eviction or matched history budgets are needed to establish how much of the advantage specifically requires cross-attention. The paper discusses such alternatives but does not evaluate them.

The claims of near-constant memory and latency need tighter qualification. Text and gist tokens continue accumulating, so memory is not bounded with stream duration. Figure 4(b) reports cumulative wall time and OOM events rather than memory trajectories or per-frame latency distributions. Moreover, caption quality is measured on approximately 20-second sports clips, leaving sustained caption quality and long-range visual recall over the much longer efficiency runs untested.

Pretrained-model adaptation does not isolate the architectural effect as cleanly as the Helium comparison. The adapted Qwen model receives substantial additional training without a similarly trained insertion control; video comparisons also use different frame budgets. The aggregate performance summaries obscure meaningful losses: Table 3 drops from 75.1 to 57.4 on InfoVQA and from 2224 to 1910 on MME relative to reproduced Qwen results. These do not invalidate the trade-off, but narrow claims about retaining the base model's capabilities.

Some explanatory conclusions exceed the ablation evidence. The five design differences are not comprehensively isolated or tested for interactions, image-token FFN updates are examined only in a smaller frozen-encoder setting, and the claimed effectiveness of gist tokens lacks a removal or capacity ablation. The experiments establish competitive configurations more convincingly than they explain the causes of the remaining performance gap.

Efficiency reproducibility is incomplete: Table 1 does not clearly specify the measurement horizon, memory units, hardware model, or full benchmarking configuration. Exact added parameter counts would also clarify comparisons by model size. The appendix reports substantial training detail, but its roughly equal end-to-end Helium training times also warrant reconciliation with the isolated throughput advantage. These reporting issues are correctable; the more consequential reservations concern streaming controls and long-duration quality.

strengths: The paper makes a useful empirical contribution under Algorithms/General: it revisits an important architectural choice through controlled comparisons, rather than relying on comparisons between differently trained models. The matched Helium1-2B experiments provide convincing evidence that simple cross-attention is more competitive with token insertion than existing cross-model results suggest.

The evaluation covers nine image benchmarks, multiple video benchmarks, and live captioning, with complementary experiments starting from a text-only LLM and adapting Qwen2.5-VL. Table 2 shows broadly competitive performance, including improvements on some general VQA tasks, while transparently identifying weaknesses on chart and infographic understanding.

The decomposition into five design differences provides a useful framework for understanding performance and efficiency. Parameter sharing, attention-layer replacement, image-token updates, and token-compression ablations offer practical guidance beyond the headline model.

The efficiency benefits are substantial in the tested settings. Table 1 reports approximately half the training memory for vanilla CA versus insertion, and much higher streaming throughput. Adapting an existing VLM while freezing its language backbone also offers a practical route to efficient multimodal deployment. Public training datasets and substantial implementation details improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The streaming comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of cross-attention from the benefit of discarding explicit visual history. The proposed model retains only the latest frame plus compressed information in text/gist tokens, whereas insertion baselines accumulate visual tokens. A matched comparison against insertion with a bounded visual cache or pruning, at comparable caption quality, is needed to establish the broader claimed advantage over practical streaming alternatives.

The long-horizon evidence primarily establishes efficiency, not sustained understanding quality. LiveSports clips are approximately 20 seconds long, while the runtime experiment extends beyond 30 minutes. There is no corresponding long-duration quality evaluation or targeted test of recalling earlier visual events. Moreover, text and gist tokens continue accumulating, so memory and attention costs are not asymptotically constant; the near-constant claim should remain explicitly tied to the measured horizon.

Performance retention is meaningfully task-dependent. In Table 3, vanilla CA drops from the reproduced Qwen baseline's 75.1 to 57.4 on InfoVQA and from 92.4 to 87.0 on DocVQA. The paper acknowledges these gaps, but does not establish their causes: the image-update experiment uses a smaller setting with a frozen encoder, and positional information and joint attention are changed together. The five-factor analysis therefore provides stronger design intuition than causal attribution.

Some comparisons and efficiency measurements need clearer qualification. The video baseline uses up to 360 frames versus 180 for the adapted models, and the original Qwen model lacks a matched continued-training control. Table 1 does not specify enough workload detail to interpret its single streaming memory/throughput point, and Figure 4(b) plots cumulative runtime rather than a memory trajectory or per-step latency. These limitations constrain the generality of the numerical claims, although they do not overturn the controlled image results.
